item.title: Stop, thoughts of sensual desire! Stop, thoughts of ill-will! Stop, thoughts of harmfulness! Enough, thoughts of sensual desire! Enough, thoughts of ill-will! Enough, thoughts of…
item.description:
Stop, thoughts of sensual desire!
Stop, thoughts of ill-will!
Stop, thoughts of harmfulness!
Enough, thoughts of sensual desire!
Enough, thoughts of ill-will!
Enough, thoughts of harmfulness!

From: Dīgha Nikāya 17 – Mahāsudassanasutta

item.title: “Furthermore, monks, with sensuality as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the basis, simply because of sensuality, taking up shields and weapons, donning…
item.description:
“Furthermore, monks, with sensuality as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the basis, simply because of sensuality, taking up shields and weapons, donning quiver and bow, they charge into battle with freshly plastered ramparts, and arrows are hurled, swords are drawn. There they are pierced by arrows, struck by spears, drenched with boiling dung, crushed by stones, and their heads are cut off by swords. There they meet death or deadly suffering. Monks, such is the peril of sensuality, a mass of suffering visible here and now, with sensuality as the cause, sensuality as the source, sensuality as the basis – simply because of sensuality.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 13 – Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta

item.title: “All conditioned things are impermanent” — When one sees this with wisdom, One becomes disenchanted with suffering — This is the path to purity. “All…
item.description:
“All conditioned things are impermanent” —
When one sees this with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

“All conditioned things are suffering” —
When one sees this with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

“All phenomena are not-self” —
When one sees this with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

From: Dhammapada 273-289

item.title: Behold this decorated image — A heap of wounds, a collection of sores, Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts, Nothing stable or permanent here.
item.description:

item.title: “Along with this suffering, abandon sensual desires, Seeking future security from bondage. Rightly understanding, with mind well liberated, There, right there, one is liberated from…
item.description:
“Along with this suffering, abandon sensual desires,
Seeking future security from bondage.
Rightly understanding, with mind well liberated,
There, right there, one is liberated from contact.
That one attains knowledge,
Accomplishes the holy life,
Reaches the end of the world,
Gets to the far shore —
That one is so called.”

From: Itivuttaka 109

item.title: “Monks, what is non-clinging and non-worry? Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple regards form as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is…
item.description:
“Monks, what is non-clinging and non-worry? Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple regards form as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ For him, that form changes and alters. When form changes and alters, no sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, or despair arise in him. He regards feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ For him, that consciousness changes and alters. When consciousness changes and alters, no sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, or despair arise in him. Thus, monks, is non-clinging and non-worry.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.8

item.title: “There are these two extremes that one who has gone forth should not pursue: devotion to sensual pleasure in sensual objects — low, vulgar, worldly,…
item.description:
“There are these two extremes that one who has gone forth should not pursue: devotion to sensual pleasure in sensual objects — low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, unbeneficial; and devotion to self-mortification — painful, ignoble, unbeneficial. Avoiding these two extremes, the Middle Way has been realized by the Tathāgata, giving rise to vision, giving rise to knowledge, leading to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, Nibbāna.

And what, headman, is that Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata, giving rise to vision, giving rise to knowledge, leading to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, Nibbāna? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This, headman, is the Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata, giving rise to vision, giving rise to knowledge, leading to peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, Nibbāna.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 42.12

item.title: Seclusion is happiness For one who knows contentment, For one who has heard the Dhamma, For one who sees rightly. Non-ill-will is happiness For those…
item.description:
Seclusion is happiness
For one who knows contentment,
For one who has heard the Dhamma,
For one who sees rightly.

Non-ill-will is happiness
For those in the world
Who practice self-restraint
Toward living beings.

Dispassion is happiness
For those who transcend sensual pleasures,
Who subdue the conceit ‘I am’ —
This is the highest happiness.

From: Udana 2.1

item.title: “For a monk practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, this is in accordance with the Dhamma: he dwells often in disenchantment toward form,…
item.description:
“For a monk practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, this is in accordance with the Dhamma: he dwells often in disenchantment toward form, toward feeling, toward perception, toward formations, toward consciousness. Dwelling often in disenchantment toward form … toward consciousness, he fully understands form … feeling … perception … formations … consciousness. By fully understanding them, he is freed from form, freed from feeling, freed from perception, freed from formations, freed from consciousness, freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is freed from suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.39
📖 Read this sutta
